props.title: Nights of Cabiria
props.initialSlug: A streetwalker seeks love in postwar Rome

sections.content: Federico Fellini's masterpiece Nights of Cabiria (1957) revolutionized character-driven storytelling through Giulietta Masina's heartbreaking portrayal of Cabiria, a Roman streetwalker maintaining dignity despite constant betrayal. Masina's expressive performance - particularly her devastating final smile - influenced generations of filmmakers exploring resilient outcasts. The film's DNA runs through later classics like Sweet Charity (1969), its direct musical adaptation, and Happy-Go-Lucky (2008), where Sally Hawkins channels Cabiria's indomitable spirit.

sections.content: The film's influence on Italian neorealism can't be overstated. While Rome, Open City (1945) and Bicycle Thieves (1948) established the movement's focus on working-class struggles, Nights of Cabiria added psychological complexity and surreal touches that bridged neorealism to the coming art house era. Fellini's signature dreamlike sequences, especially Cabiria's nightclub hypnosis scene, paved the way for the surreal character studies of 8½ (1963) and Persona (1966).

Modern filmmakers continue drawing from Cabiria's well. Leaving Las Vegas (1995) echoes its mix of darkness and redemption, while Monster (2003) and In the Cut (2003) explore similar themes of vulnerable women navigating dangerous urban spaces. The film's greatest legacy may be its humanitarian gaze - treating marginalized characters with empathy and complexity decades before it became common practice. movies.title: Vivre Sa Vie
movies.slug: Godard's stark portrait of a Parisian woman's descent into prostitution, told in 12 tableaux

sections.content: Post-Cabiria films about sex workers shifted from moral judgment to character complexity. Klute (1971) and Pretty Woman (1990) show this evolution, though none match Fellini's delicate balance of tragedy and hope. Recent entries like Tangerine (2015) and Never Rarely Sometimes Always (2020) inherit Cabiria's intimate, judgment-free approach to marginalized characters.
